## Design

### 2026-10-28: ## SOOOOOOO I  just wrapped up a massive session and trust me my brain is completely fried rn. But I finally finished the full schematic for the camera and tbvh it was a hell of a ride to complete it.

**3.8h**

## SOOOOOOO I  just wrapped up a massive session and trust me my brain is completely fried rn. But I finally finished the full schematic for the camera and tbvh it was a hell of a ride to complete it.
now i started the sessions and spent my hours like this: I spent the first solid hour just deep in the trenches researching parts and mapping out the hardware architecture. I needed to keep the whole build under $30 while finding the right parts that actually fit's the project. I tried to find through hole modules and beginner friendly SMD parts. Trying to figure out the right MOSFETs and transistors was a massive rabbit hole. I had to read actual datasheets to figure out how to safely drive a high power "6-LED 850nm IR ring" without completely frying the "ESP32-S3-CAM". That led me to the "AO3400 N-Channel MOSFET" for the heavy lifting. I also had to calculate the exact 33 ohm resistor values for the LEDs so they would run perfectly off 5V. On top of that, checking and double checking the ESP32 pinout took forever because half of the GPIOs are already used by the built in camera and SD card slot.
---
## Right out the gate, I dropped all my power symbols onto the canvas and then just completely forgot to wire the actual power management circuit together. I literally tried moving on to the thermal sensor while my TP4056 battery input and AMS1117 voltage regulator were just floating in the void doing absolutely nothing. I had to backtrack, fix that, and make sure I added the 10uF bulk capacitors so the ESP32 wouldn't brown out during wifi spikes.
Also  I dropped generic pins for the MLX90614 thermal sensor instead of proper female sockets. Electrically it didn't really matter, but it bothered my ocd so I spent time hot swapping the symbols. Also, I couldn't find the standard 2N2222 transistor for my laser switch in the default KiCad library anywhere. I spent like 20 minutes googling workarounds before I ended up pivoting to the S8050 NPN instead. Honestly it works just as well for switching the laser and handling the PWM dimming for the TFT screen backlight, but it was annoying to redesign on the fly.
Wiring up the TFT screen took a chunky amount of time too. Connecting the SPI bus meant individually routing MOSI, SCK, CS, DC, and RST labels and making sure my schematic didn't look like a plate of spaghetti.
The absolute most annoying problem of the night was a stupid typo that had me staring at the screen for way too long. I routed my ESP32 header pins with the labels i2s_sda and i2s_scl, but I labeled the actual thermal sensor i2c_sda. Because KiCad is insanely strict about exact string matches, that single letter difference meant my brain and sensor weren't even connected. Caught it just in time before I finalized the board, but finding it was a headache.
But i won't say it was all struggles. I glided smoothly while designing the tactical control buttons. I originally planned to use physical 100nF debounce capacitors for all four buttons. halfway through wiring them up I realized I could just use internal pullups in the ESP32 code later. SO  i removed the capacitors and wired the buttons straight to ground.

## Overall, the schematic is 100% complete and hopefully works lol

### 2026-10-30: ### Devlog #2: The Placement Phase

**1.8h**

### Devlog #2: The Placement Phase

I just wrapped up the physical layout for the  camera. I spent like 1.8in the KiCad PCB editor today, and about 1.5 hours of that was just shifting components around to get the mechanics right.

## TheBoard shape
When I first imported the schematic, KiCad generated a dense rat's nest of overlapping THT and SMD footprints. My very first step was drawing a clean 90x60mm Edge.Cuts board outline with rounded corners to establish a proper camera form factor.

## UI Layout:
The hardest part was visualizing the layout in 3D. Since this requires a point and shoot design, I couldn't just leave everything on the top side.
1) I flipped the 2.4-inch TFT LCD and the tactile push-buttons to the B.Cu (back copper) layer.
2) I customized my UI layout slightly from the standard approach, putting the LCD on the right and stacking the control SW components on the left to better suit my grip.
2) I constantly toggled the 3D viewer to check mechanical clearances, ensuring the back of the LCD glass panel wouldn't collide with any SMD components placed on the front side.

## Custom Power Rules
I spent up the last 20min setting up DRC parameters, which actually ended up saving the board. While reading through an engineering forum about pcb routing techniques, I learned about IPC standards for trace current capacity. I realized that the high current drawn by the 6-LED IR array would cause KiCad's default copper traces to overheat and delaminate.

To fix this, I navigated into the board setup and created a custom power net class. I assigned the +5V, +3V3, and gnd nets to a much thicker 0.6mm track width so they can safely handle it

### 2026-10-31: # #Routed the Main PCB both sides

**2h**

# #Routed the Main PCB both sides
##  Main issues I ran into:
1) parts short circuiting.  i had a couple of traces crossing paths that weren’t supposed to connect. Had to go back and reroute them on separate layers to keep things isolated properly.
2) some of my components were overlapping. A few parts were placed too close to each other, overlapping footprints basically. so i had to shift placements around and redo some of the routing after moving things, which ate up extra time.

## how i fixed them:
1) rerouted the shorted traces, and then ran drc to make sure
2) repositioned overlapping components with proper spacing this time, then rewired them
3) ran a final DRC to make sure nothing else was flagged

### 2026-11-01: # # Completed the FIRMWARE

**2.2h**

# # Completed the FIRMWARE

## What the code does:
### - Handles a handheld device with a live camera feed from an OV3660 sensor pushed straight to an ILI9341 screen, a thermal sensor overlay showing object temperature, a laser toggle, an IR LED toggle for night vision, a button to cycle HUD text color between red, green and white, and a shutter button that right now just triggers a buzzer beep. (this was formalized by ai for better use of words)
---
# What’s still missing:
1) no actual photo/video saving yet
2) no real debounce separation between the four buttons, they all share one timer right now, so when 2 buttons are mashed, they may overlap and one button may not register
---
# The annoying part:
## Every time I went back to check the code, something had subtly broken it.

1) first when i was creating the configs, a stray chunk of text that got inserted ( by autocomplete) into the middle of a camera config line, it was always breaking for sure.
2) then variable names stopped matching themselves, I’d declare something as hud_color_index in one spot and then referenced it as hudcolorindex everywhere else, which doesn’t compile since those are two different variables.
3) then a whole FCKING config line for the camera’s HREF pin vanished entirely while editing the hud code
---
## These errors took a hell lot of time to fix, while the logic also took a ton of time, as i have experice with C++ but not that much, i used stackoverflow, youtube and some ai to clearup some errors and sanity check the code.
---
## Once that was sorted:
### The actual logic seems fine ( i think so). pin assignments avoid the reserved PSRAM and strapping pins on the ESP32-S3, buttons are mapped to GPIO4 through 7, camera data lines are on GPIO33, 34, 38 through 41, 47 and 48, and I2C is shared between the thermal sensor and the camera’s "sccb" bus without conflict.
